cards.title: M1 · Decision Map — Separable, Linear, Both, or Neither?
cards.why: The ten-second triage from Part 4 — one picture that replaces memorizing two recipes.
cards.prompt: Create a flat-vector educational flowchart titled "First-Order ODE Triage". Layout top to bottom: start box reading "dy/dx = ?". Decision diamond 1: "Do y and y' appear only to the first power, never inside functions, never multiplied together?" YES branch goes right to a green box: "LINEAR → standard form y' + P(x)y = f(x) → μ = e^∫P dx". Continue down to decision diamond 2: "Does the right side factor as g(x)·f(y)?" YES branch goes right to a teal box: "SEPARABLE → dy/f(y) = g(x) dx → integrate both sides". A path where both answers are YES leads to a box "BOTH — pick the easier route"; both NO leads to a grey box "NEITHER (needs other tools)". Along the bottom, four small example chips: "y' = xy + x → both", "y' + x²y = x³ → linear only", "yy' = x → separable only", "y' = sin(x+y) → neither".

cards.title: M3 · The Integrating Factor — Why μ Works
cards.why: The single most-lost mark in 2.3: students memorize μ without seeing the collapse into (μy)′.
cards.prompt: Create a flat-vector educational diagram titled "The Integrating Factor: Why μ Works". Two large panels. Left panel "THE PROBLEM": equation "y' + P(x)y = f(x)" with the left side circled in red, caption "not the derivative of anything — cannot integrate directly". Right panel "THE TRICK": the same equation with every term multiplied by a glowing teal highlighted factor "μ = e^∫P dx", and a big arrow showing the left side collapsing into one compact box "(μy)'", with a verification bubble: "product-rule check: (μy)' = μy' + μ'y = μy' + μPy ✓". Bottom strip: five small numbered chips in a row: "1 standard form" → "2 μ = e^∫P dx" → "3 multiply every term" → "4 integrate: μy = ∫μf dx + C" → "5 divide by μ".

cards.title: M5 · The Linearity Courtroom — Three Laws
cards.why: Directly from your study guide's legal lens: y on trial, t always innocent. Makes the test unforgettable.
cards.prompt: Create a flat-vector educational infographic titled "The Linearity Courtroom: y is on trial, t is innocent". Three vertical law panels side by side, each topped with a small gavel icon. LAW 1 panel titled "First power only": green check examples "y, y', 5y''" and red cross examples "y², (y')³, √y". LAW 2 panel titled "Never inside another function": green check "sin(t) + y" and red crosses "sin(t+y), e^y, ln(y')". LAW 3 panel titled "y-terms never multiply": green check "t² · y'" and red crosses "y · y', y · y''". A dark footer banner across the bottom reading: "Verdict: ONE guilty term convicts the whole equation. Functions of t alone (t², sin t) are ALWAYS innocent."

cards.title: M6 · Piecewise Forcing — Continuity at the Seam
cards.why: The capstone L5: watching the charge-then-drain curve is what makes 'stitch by continuity' click.
cards.prompt: Generate this figure by running Python (matplotlib) — do NOT draw it as an illustration. Plot the solution of y' + y = f(x), y(0) = 0, where f(x) = 1 on [0,1] and f(x) = 0 for x > 1: that is y = 1 − e^(−x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and y = (e − 1)e^(−x) for x > 1, over x in [0, 4]. One continuous teal curve with a vertical dashed grey line at x = 1 and a dot at the junction (1, 0.632). Annotate "charging: y rises toward 1" on the first segment and "draining: exponential decay" on the second. Below the main axes add a small inset axes showing the step function f(x) jumping from 1 to 0 at x = 1. Title: "Piecewise forcing: y is continuous, y' is not". White background, axes labeled x and y, clean academic style.

cards.title: M7 · Finite Blow-Up — Interval of Validity
cards.why: S5's deepest idea: a tame-looking equation whose solution escapes in finite time.
cards.prompt: Generate this figure by running Python (matplotlib) — do NOT draw it as an illustration. Plot y = 2/(1 − 2 sin x) on the open interval (−7π/6, π/6), the solution of y' = y² cos x with y(0) = 2. Mark the point (0, 2) with a dot labeled "y(0) = 2". Draw vertical dashed asymptotes at x = −7π/6 and x = π/6, each labeled "blow-up". Lightly shade the regions outside the interval in pale red with the caption "outside the interval of validity". Title: "A nonlinear solution can escape in finite time". White background, axes labeled, y-axis limited to [−1, 10].

Equal aspect ratio, axes labeled, white background.

cards.title: E1 · The Three Laws Poster

cards.prompt: Create a flat-vector educational poster titled "The Three Laws of Circuit Analysis". Three equal panels side by side, each with a clean flat circuit schematic using zigzag resistors. Left side: a flat series circuit with a source "Vs" and two zigzag resistors "R1" and "R2", with "+ V2 −" marked across R2. Right side: one horizontal bar labeled "Vs" split into two segments proportional to R1 and R2; the R2 segment highlighted in teal and labeled "V2 = Vs · R2 / (R1 + R2)". Caption under the bar: "split by resistance ratio — R_target over R_TOTAL, never R_target over the other resistor". Small example chip at the bottom: "24 V across 4 kΩ + 8 kΩ → V2 = 16 V".

Left side: two parallel vertical branches between two rails holding zigzag resistors "R1" and "R2"; a total current arrow "I" enters the top node and splits into "I1" and "I2". Right side: a horizontal bar labeled "I" split into two segments where the SMALLER resistor's branch gets the BIGGER segment; the I2 segment highlighted in teal, labeled "I2 = I · R1 / (R1 + R2)". cards.title: E5 · Ladder Reduction — The P4 Collapse, Step by Step
cards.why: The exact P4 network from your practice set, collapsed far-to-near in four frames.
cards.prompt: Generate this figure by running Python with the schemdraw library — do NOT draw it as an illustration. Draw a four-panel sequence showing the collapse of this ladder circuit (12 V source on the left; R1 = 3k from node A to the bottom rail; R2 = 2k from A to node B; R3 = 6k from B to the bottom rail; R4 = 6k from B to node C; R5 = 12k and R6 = 12k from C to the bottom rail). Panel 1: the full circuit with the R5 ∥ R6 pair highlighted, caption "Step 1 — 12k ∥ 12k = 6k". Panel 2: the pair replaced by one 6k resistor now in series with R4, caption "Step 2 — 6k + 6k = 12k". Panel 3: that whole branch in parallel with R3, then in series with R2, captions "Step 3 — 12k ∥ 6k = 4k" and "Step 4 — 2k + 4k = 6k". Panel 4: the final parallel with R1, caption "Req = 3k ∥ 6k = 2k, so Is = 12 V / 2k = 6 mA". Every resistor labeled with its value, clean flat schematic style.

cards.title: E6 · Nodal Analysis — KCL Writes Itself
cards.why: Method (a) of the flagship problem: once node voltages are the unknowns, each current is just ΔV/R.
cards.prompt: Create a flat-vector educational diagram titled "Nodal Analysis: Every Current is a Voltage Difference over a Resistance". Center: a flat circuit fragment with two node dots labeled "VB" and "VC", one zigzag resistor "R4" between them, one resistor "R1" from VB up to a rail marked "12 V", and resistors "R3" and "R5" from VB and VC down to a ground rail. Curved arrows on each branch labeled with fractions: "(VB − 12)/R1" flowing in from the source, "VB/R3" flowing down, "(VB − VC)/R4" flowing across. A boxed equation beneath: "KCL at B: (VB − 12)/R1 + VB/R3 + (VB − VC)/R4 = 0". Caption: "choose node voltages as unknowns → one KCL per node → the system writes itself".

cards.title: E7 · Voltage Source vs Current Source
cards.why: P5's key idea: a current source's voltage is an output — students constantly treat it as an input.
cards.prompt: Create a flat-vector educational diagram titled "Voltage Source vs Current Source: Who Decides What". Two panels. Left panel: a battery symbol labeled "12 V" connected to a grey box labeled "any resistor network"; beneath it two rows: "FIXES: the voltage across itself" and "current = whatever the circuit pulls". Right panel: a current-source circle with an upward arrow labeled "6 mA" feeding the same grey network box; beneath it: "FIXES: the current through itself" and "voltage = whatever the circuit needs — find it from Req!". A dark banner across the bottom: "A current source's voltage is an OUTPUT, not an input."

cards.title: E8 · The Engineer's Triangle — V · mA · kΩ
cards.why: The units discipline from your recipe cards: these three units never produce powers of ten.
cards.prompt: Create a flat-vector educational diagram titled "The Engineer's Triangle: V · mA · kΩ". Center: a large triangle with "V" at the top vertex and "mA" and "kΩ" at the bottom two vertices, styled like the classic V=IR triangle. Three arrows leading out to small panels: first "V = mA × kΩ" with example "2 mA × 8 kΩ = 16 V"; second "mA = V / kΩ" with example "12 V / 3 kΩ = 4 mA"; third "kΩ = V / mA" with example "7.2 V / 6 mA = 1.2 kΩ". Footer caption: "these three units are self-consistent — convert Ω and A BEFORE you start, then no powers of ten ever appear mid-calculation".
